findings.claim: `definite?: boolean | undefined` is a tri-state flag whose absence must be interpreted as `true` ("definite"), which is the opposite of the natural `if (!fn.definite)` / falsy check most consumers will write.
findings.rationale: The doc comment says the field is "False when this function's INVALID does not strictly mean 'the runtime would reject'", i.e. the safe/normal case is `true` and the special case is `false`. But the property is optional, so every compiled function produced before/outside the new code path (and any wrapper that forgets to set it) will have `definite === undefined`. Any call site using a falsy test (`if (!fn.definite)`, `fn.definite ?? false`, `definite: a.definite && b.definite`) will then silently classify definite functions as indefinite, changing behavior for existing callers. Making it required, or defaulting explicitly via `fn.definite !== false`, would remove the ambiguity. I can't see the call sites in this hunk, so this is a suspected rather than confirmed bug — worth checking every read of `.definite`.

findings.claim: `definite` is an optional mutable property bolted onto the function object, so it is easy to drop when compiled functions are wrapped/re-created (the same hazard the existing `code` property has).
findings.rationale: Anywhere the compiler composes or re-wraps a `CompiledFn` (e.g. building a new closure and copying `code` onto it), the new `definite` flag must be propagated too; the optional type gives no compile-time signal when it is forgotten, and the loss is silent because `undefined` is a legal value. Confidence is moderate — it depends on how many wrapping sites exist in this file, which is not visible here.
